items.prompt: How does a single, soft-bodied coral polyp end up producing the hard, rock-like structure of a reef?

options.label: It gathers grains of sand and cements them together with mucus
options.feedback: A polyp doesn't build its structure out of gathered sand; it manufactures the hard material itself, from minerals dissolved in the surrounding water.

options.label: It draws dissolved minerals out of the seawater and secretes them as a hard limestone cup around its own soft body
options.feedback: A coral polyp pulls calcium and carbonate ions dissolved in the seawater around it and combines them into solid limestone, which it secretes at its base as a hard cup that protects and supports its soft body.

options.label: It borrows an empty shell left behind by another sea creature
options.feedback: A polyp does not occupy a shell built by something else; the hard structure beneath it is one it produces itself.

options.label: It hardens its own skin permanently into rock over time
options.feedback: The polyp's own body stays soft; the hard material is a separate mineral structure it builds and sits within, not its skin turning to stone.

items.ok_title: Built from what's dissolved in the water
items.ko_line: Ask where the hard material actually comes from, given that the polyp itself stays soft.
items.exp_title: A soft animal, a hard house
items.exp_text: Seawater carries dissolved calcium and carbonate, and a coral polyp draws these in and combines them into solid calcium carbonate — the mineral that makes up limestone. It secretes this material at its base, building a hard cup it sits inside and can retreat into. As thousands of polyps in a colony each add their own small cup side by side, and older cups are built upon by new ones, the combined structure grows into the rock of a reef.

items.prompt: Why do reefs mostly grow in warm, shallow, clear water in the tropics rather than in cold or murky seas?

options.label: Cold water is too dense for a polyp's skeleton to form properly
options.feedback: Water density doesn't prevent a polyp from secreting its skeleton; the real constraint is the light and warmth the polyp and its partners need.

options.label: Reefs simply have not had time to spread to colder regions yet
options.feedback: Reef-building corals have existed for an immense stretch of time, long enough to have spread anywhere the conditions suited them; the limit is environmental, not a lack of time.

options.label: Murky water carries too many nutrients, which overfeed and kill young polyps
options.feedback: It isn't excess nutrients that stops reefs from growing in murky water — it's that murkiness blocks the light on which the coral depends, through the algae living inside it.

options.label: Building a limestone skeleton runs faster in warmth, and the coral depends on sunlight reaching it clearly for the energy that powers that building
options.feedback: Secreting a limestone skeleton is helped along by warmer water, and reef-building coral gets much of its energy from tiny algae living inside its tissue that need clear, shallow, sunlit water to photosynthesise — so cold, deep or murky water starves the whole partnership of what it needs.

items.ok_title: Warmth for building, light for feeding
items.ok_line: Two needs, both met only near the sunlit surface of a warm sea.
items.ko_line: Think about what the coral itself needs both to build its skeleton and to get its energy.
items.exp_title: Needing both warmth and light at once
items.exp_text: Secreting a limestone skeleton happens far more readily in warm water than in cold. At the same time, reef-building coral hosts tiny photosynthesising algae inside its own tissue, and those algae need clear, shallow water for enough sunlight to reach them. Where water is cold, deep or clouded with sediment, either the skeleton-building slows, the algae go hungry for light, or both — which is why reefs cluster in warm, clear, shallow tropical seas rather than spreading everywhere the ocean reaches.

items.prompt: What is the relationship between a coral polyp and the tiny algae that live inside its tissue?

options.label: The algae photosynthesise and share the sugars they make with the coral, while the coral provides them shelter and nutrients in return
options.feedback: Living inside the coral's tissue, the algae use sunlight to photosynthesise and pass a large share of the sugars they produce on to their host, while the coral in turn shelters them and supplies nutrients they need — each partner supporting the other.

options.label: The algae are simply parasites that the coral tolerates but gains nothing from
options.feedback: A coral without its algae typically weakens and starves rather than benefiting from their absence, which shows the coral genuinely depends on what the algae provide.

options.label: The coral eats the algae outright as its main source of food
options.feedback: The coral generally keeps its algae alive and productive rather than consuming them; it lives off the sugars they release while they continue photosynthesising.

options.label: The algae live on the outside of the coral's skeleton rather than inside its tissue
options.feedback: The algae live inside the coral's own soft tissue, not attached to the outside of its skeleton, which is what lets the coral shelter them so closely.

items.ok_line: Sugar for shelter, in both directions.
items.ko_line: Ask what each side actually gives the other, rather than assuming one side simply exploits the other.
items.exp_title: A partnership, not a one-way arrangement
items.exp_text: Tiny algae live embedded within a coral polyp's own tissue, sheltered from the open water and supplied with nutrients the coral releases as waste. In return, the algae photosynthesise using sunlight and pass a large portion of the sugars they produce directly to the coral, which relies on that steady supply of food to grow and to build its skeleton. Each partner depends on what the other provides.

items.prompt: What actually happens to a coral when unusually warm water causes it to 'bleach' and turn pale?

options.label: The heat dissolves the coral's limestone skeleton directly
options.feedback: Bleaching is about colour and the loss of the coral's algae, not the skeleton dissolving away, though a starved coral can weaken over time as a result.

options.label: Sunlight burns the pigment out of the coral's own tissue, like a sunburn
options.feedback: The coral's colour comes mainly from the algae living within it, not from a separate pigment in its own tissue that heat could simply burn away.

options.label: Heat stress disrupts the algae living inside the coral, and the coral expels them, losing both its colour and its main source of food
options.feedback: Under prolonged heat stress, the photosynthesising algae inside a coral begin to malfunction, and the coral responds by expelling them from its tissue — which removes the colour they provided and, with it, the steady supply of sugars the coral had been living on.

options.label: Cold water rushing in from the deep ocean washes the colour away
options.feedback: Bleaching is triggered by unusually warm water stressing the coral's algae, not by an inrush of cold water.

items.ok_line: The algae falter under heat, and the coral lets them go.
items.ko_line: Remember where the coral's colour actually comes from, and think about what heat does to that source.
items.exp_text: A coral's vivid colour comes almost entirely from the algae living inside its tissue, not from the coral itself. When water stays too warm for too long, those algae stop functioning properly and can start producing substances harmful to their host, so the coral expels them from its tissue as a defence. Without the algae, the coral is left pale and, having lost its main source of food along with its colour, it can starve if the stress continues.

items.prompt: What is the difference between how a fringing reef and a barrier reef sit relative to the coastline they grow near?

options.label: A fringing reef grows directly attached to the shore, while a barrier reef stands separated from the shore by a stretch of open lagoon
options.feedback: A fringing reef builds outward right from the coastline itself with no gap behind it, while a barrier reef has grown far enough offshore, or the land behind it has sunk far enough, that a wide lagoon of open water now separates the reef from the coast.

options.label: A fringing reef only forms around volcanic islands, and a barrier reef only forms around continents
options.feedback: Both types of reef can form near either continents or islands; the real difference is whether a lagoon separates the reef from the shore, not what kind of land it borders.

options.label: A barrier reef is simply a fringing reef that has been renamed once it grows large enough
options.feedback: Size alone doesn't turn one into the other; what changes is the presence of a lagoon between the reef and the shore, which reflects a real difference in how each formed.

options.label: A fringing reef grows in deep water, while a barrier reef grows only in shallow water
options.feedback: Both types grow in the shallow, sunlit water reef-building coral needs; their difference lies in their distance from the coast, not in water depth generally.

items.ok_title: Attached, or set apart by a lagoon
items.ok_line: The gap behind it is what tells the two apart.
items.ko_line: Ask what lies between the reef and the coastline in each case.
items.exp_title: Right at the shore, or set apart from it
items.exp_text: A fringing reef begins growing directly out from the coastline, with no significant gap behind it. A barrier reef, by contrast, has either grown far enough out from the original shore, or has kept pace with land slowly sinking behind it, that a broad stretch of open lagoon now lies between the living reef and the coast. The presence of that lagoon is what separates the two, not their size or the type of land they border.

items.prompt: How does a ring-shaped atoll, with open lagoon at its centre and no volcanic island left in sight, come to form?

options.label: An atoll is carved out directly by ocean currents circling a single spot
options.feedback: Currents shape sediment locally but cannot carve a limestone ring the size of an atoll; the ring is built by living coral growth, not cut by moving water.

options.label: A meteor strikes the open ocean and coral later grows around the resulting crater's rim
options.feedback: Atolls form through a gradual process of coral growth around a sinking volcanic island, not around a crater left by an impact.

options.label: A fringing reef begins growing around a volcanic island, and as the island slowly sinks and erodes away over a very long time, the reef keeps growing upward, leaving a ring behind
options.feedback: Coral first grows as a fringing reef right around the base of a young volcanic island, and as that island gradually sinks beneath the waves and erodes away over an immense stretch of time, the living reef keeps building upward to stay near the sunlit surface, so that once the island itself has vanished, only the ring of reef it grew around is left standing.

options.label: Sand blown by wind piles up naturally into a ring shape on the open ocean surface
options.feedback: Sand cannot pile itself into a stable ring on open water with no underlying structure; an atoll's ring is built from coral growth around a sinking island, not from windblown sand.

items.ok_title: A ring left behind by a vanished island
items.ok_line: The reef kept climbing as the island beneath it disappeared.
items.ko_line: Ask what the reef was originally growing around, and what happened to that thing over a very long stretch of time.
items.exp_title: Outliving the island it grew around
items.exp_text: Coral first establishes itself as a fringing reef hugging the shore of a newly formed volcanic island. Over an immense stretch of time, that island slowly sinks and wears away, but the living reef keeps building itself upward, staying close to the sunlit surface it depends on rather than sinking with the rock beneath it. By the time the island has disappeared entirely below the surface, all that remains is the ring of reef that once grew around its edge, now enclosing an open lagoon where the island used to stand.

items.prompt: Why does a coral reef tend to grow mainly upward, toward the surface, rather than simply spreading outward and downward into deeper water?

options.label: The coral, and the algae living within it, depend on sunlit, shallow water, so growth is drawn toward staying near the surface as conditions around it change
options.feedback: Reef-building coral relies on light-hungry algae living in its tissue, and both partners fare poorly once they sink too far from the sunlit surface, so as sea level rises or the ground beneath a reef slowly subsides, the coral that survives and keeps building is the coral that manages to grow upward and stay near the light.

options.label: Coral polyps physically cannot attach themselves at any real depth
options.feedback: Coral can settle and grow at a range of depths where enough light reaches; it isn't a fixed physical limit on attachment that drives upward growth, but the ongoing need to stay near sunlight.

options.label: Predators are more common in deeper water, so coral avoids growing there
options.feedback: The upward growth of a reef is explained by its need for sunlight reaching the algae within it, not primarily by avoiding predators in deeper water.

options.label: Ocean currents are too strong near the seabed for coral to survive there
options.feedback: Coral reefs can withstand a range of current strengths; it is the loss of sunlight with depth, not current strength, that limits how deep a reef can grow and keeps its growth directed upward.

items.ok_title: Chasing the light, not the depth
items.ok_line: Growth follows wherever the sunlight still reaches.
items.ko_line: Think about what the coral's algae actually need, and what happens to that need as depth increases.
items.exp_title: Staying within reach of the light
items.exp_text: A coral reef's growth is powered largely by the light-dependent algae living inside its polyps, and those algae need to stay within the sunlit upper layer of the ocean to keep photosynthesising. As sea level rises, or as the ground supporting a reef slowly subsides, coral sitting too far below the surface receives too little light and struggles, while coral that manages to build upward stays within reach of the sun. Over time, that ongoing pressure to remain near the light is what steers a healthy reef's growth mainly upward.

items.prompt: Why does the water around a thriving coral reef often look strikingly clear and blue, despite supporting such a dense concentration of life?

options.label: Reef life is thin and sparse compared with other parts of the ocean, leaving little to cloud the water
options.feedback: A reef actually supports an unusually dense concentration of life for its size; the clarity of the water isn't because there is little life there.

options.label: Storms regularly flush the area and wash any cloudiness out to open sea
options.feedback: Storms are occasional events, but reef water tends to stay clear even during long calm stretches, which points to an ongoing mechanism rather than periodic flushing.

options.label: Nutrients are captured and recycled tightly within reef organisms' own tissue rather than drifting loose in the surrounding water
options.feedback: In a reef, nutrients released by one organism are very often taken up almost immediately by another living nearby, so instead of drifting freely in the water where they would feed the drifting plant-like organisms that cloud murkier seas, most of the reef's nutrients stay locked within living tissue, leaving the water around it clear.

options.label: The limestone of the reef itself bleaches the surrounding water white and clear
options.feedback: Limestone doesn't chemically bleach seawater; the clarity comes from how tightly nutrients are held within reef life rather than left free in the water.

items.ok_line: Nutrients pass from one living thing to the next before they ever cloud the water.
items.ko_line: Ask what usually makes ocean water look cloudy, and why that might not be happening here.
items.exp_title: Nutrients kept close, not left drifting
items.exp_text: Water usually turns cloudy where nutrients drift freely and feed a haze of tiny floating organisms. On a reef, though, nutrients released by one organism are typically captured and used again almost immediately by a neighbour, whether coral, algae, or something else living close by, rather than escaping into the open water. Because so little nutrient is left loose to fuel that clouding growth, the water around a healthy reef stays clear even while supporting an unusually dense concentration of life.

items.prompt: How does extra carbon dioxide dissolving into seawater make it harder for coral to build its limestone skeleton?

options.label: The dissolved gas physically fills the pores of the skeleton, blocking new growth
options.feedback: The problem isn't gas physically clogging the skeleton; it's a chemical shift in the water that makes building new limestone harder in the first place.

options.label: Dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with the water to form a weak acid, which lowers the water's pH and reduces the carbonate ions coral needs to build its skeleton
options.feedback: When carbon dioxide dissolves into seawater, it reacts with it to form carbonic acid, and that shifts the water's chemistry toward being more acidic while also reducing the concentration of carbonate ions available — the very ions coral needs to combine with calcium to build its limestone skeleton.

options.label: The extra gas heats the water, and heat alone is what stops the skeleton from forming
options.feedback: Dissolved carbon dioxide changes the water's chemistry directly; it is the shift in acidity and carbonate availability that hinders skeleton-building, not a warming effect from the gas itself.

options.label: Carbon dioxide feeds the coral's algae so heavily that the coral itself is starved of carbonate
options.feedback: The effect on skeleton-building comes from a direct chemical shift in the water's carbonate availability, not from the algae outcompeting the coral for food.

items.ok_title: A chemical shift, not a physical block
items.ok_line: More acidic water leaves less carbonate for the coral to build with.
items.ko_line: Think about what dissolved carbon dioxide actually does to the chemistry of the water itself.
items.exp_text: When carbon dioxide dissolves into seawater, it doesn't just sit there — it reacts with the water to form carbonic acid, nudging the water's chemistry to be more acidic than before. That shift also reduces the amount of carbonate ion dissolved and available in the water, and carbonate is exactly what coral needs, combined with calcium, to secrete its limestone skeleton. With less carbonate on hand, building that skeleton takes more effort and proceeds more slowly.

items.prompt: Why don't coral reefs generally grow near the mouths of large rivers, even where the water is warm enough?

options.label: River mouths are always too deep for coral to reach the surface
options.feedback: Depth at a river mouth isn't the general obstacle; many river mouths are shallow, but the fresh water they release still keeps coral away.

options.label: Rivers carry too much oxygen, which is toxic to coral polyps
options.feedback: Oxygen in the water isn't harmful to coral; the real obstacle where rivers meet the sea is fresh water diluting the salt level the coral and its algae depend on.

options.label: There simply isn't enough sunlight near a river mouth for coral to grow
options.feedback: Light levels near a river mouth vary and aren't the main obstacle by themselves; it's the fresh water lowering the surrounding salinity that keeps reefs away, often along with sediment blocking what light there is.

options.label: Coral and its algae need a fairly narrow, steady salt level, and the fresh water pouring from a river dilutes the sea nearby too much and too unpredictably for them to thrive
options.feedback: Reef-building coral, and the algae living within it, are adapted to the fairly steady salinity of the open sea, and a large river constantly releases fresh water that dilutes the salt level nearby far below what they need, and in an unpredictable, fluctuating way that leaves little chance for either partner to adjust.

items.ok_title: Diluted beyond what it can tolerate
items.ok_line: Fresh water pouring in keeps the salt level too low and too unsteady.
items.ko_line: Think about what a large river actually adds to the sea around its mouth, and what the coral depends on in the water it lives in.
items.exp_title: A salt level rivers keep disturbing
items.exp_text: Reef-building coral and its algae are adapted to the fairly steady salinity of open, undiluted seawater. A large river releases a constant flow of fresh water into the sea near its mouth, and that steady inflow lowers the surrounding salt level well below what the coral and its algae are suited to, while also fluctuating with rain and season in a way that gives neither partner a stable range to adjust to. Warm water alone isn't enough to support a reef where the salinity keeps being diluted this way.
